corrections.issue: Direction is incomplete: for the rally case Crabel says large traders stopping a rally dead with high volume is not a place to buy, but for the decline case (market goes down, dead stops, narrow range, high volume) he says someone is standing in front of the move, which means selling into that stall is unattractive, not that one should not buy.
corrections.fix: Wyckoff effort versus result (effort = volume, result = price range): high volume with a narrow range at a dead stop shows a large trader absorbing flow; after a rally it is a poor place to buy, and at a low it signals someone standing in front of the move (do not chase the decline).

corrections.issue: Overstated: Crabel says high-frequency groups are the liquidity backbone, like the old floor traders, make money and need to spend millions for microseconds, and he does not begrudge them; he does not say they leave short-term managers' alpha untouched (he notes some nuances are a little frustrating).
corrections.fix: Toby Crabel: high-frequency firms are the liquidity backbone, comparable to floor traders, and will make money; they spend millions of dollars for a few microseconds of speed, whereas the firm prefers to invest in cheaper execution edge, while acknowledging some frustrating nuances.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker for one element: the remark that the 200-day moving average has become much more important is a host's inference ('I guess') after Crabel said the short-term moves are generally with the trend; Crabel did not say it.
corrections.fix: Toby Crabel: the current environment resembles the 1970s (debasement, gold and silver, profitable trend following, large abrupt moves) but is bigger and global. Host (inference): the 200-day moving average may have become more important.

corrections.issue: Imprecise: Crabel says that apart from an earlier period (caption garbled as '60 to 1962') which was one of the worst for this strategy, the last two or three years have been equally as bad; this is not simply 'worst in decades'.
corrections.fix: Opening range breakout has deteriorated: the last two or three years have been as bad as one earlier worst period (year garbled in the captions), because 24-hour sessions make the open impossible to determine, a dissipation first seen in the 1980s with US Treasury night sessions.

completeness_estimate: 0.8 - the first reader caught the core edge-decay, execution, generalised-strategy, volume-effort and replication ideas; misses are supporting caveats and data points (zero-commission origin, session-structure test of ORB, publication persistence, volume comparability, debasement anecdote) and four speaker or direction misreads.
